systems.name: Enterprise AI Assistant: Integration Layers at Scale
systems.headline: One employee request. Four integration layers.
systems.discoverySection: Ask the Five Questions That Reshape the Design
systems.description: Coordinate enterprise applications while each application retains its own permission checks.
systems.question: Schedule a meeting with John and send him the latest proposal.
systems.scope: This design covers integration and tool discovery. RAG, memory and human-approval workflows are not implemented here.
systems.provenance: Architecture, requirements and boundaries are adapted from the named canonical Markdown. Scenario branches, identifiers and payloads are illustrative teaching examples, not executions or measured results. Source assumptions remain assumptions.

discovery.question: Read-only, or can it act?
discovery.answer: The source requires reads and writes.
discovery.decision: Keep authorisation at every application boundary and trace side effects.

discovery.question: Do backends already speak REST?
discovery.answer: The estate mixes REST, GraphQL, SOAP and legacy SQL.
discovery.decision: Use connectors and MCP discovery over the transports the applications actually support.

discovery.question: Multi-step requests?
discovery.answer: Yes: scheduling and sharing span two domains.
discovery.decision: Use a planner for multi-step work; simple tasks need no planning framework.

discovery.question: Scale?
discovery.answer: The scenario assumes 50,000 employees and roughly 8,000 concurrent requests at peak.
discovery.decision: Keep request services stateless, bound work, and grow tool discovery selectively.

discovery.question: Does every employee see the same data?
discovery.answer: No. Finance and HR have different access.
discovery.decision: Propagate verified identity and enforce source permissions.

scenarios.label: Meeting and proposal succeed
scenarios.outcome: The calendar booked the meeting and the document application shared the proposal.

stages.title: Authenticate the employee and admit the request
stages.what: An employee asks to meet John and send the latest proposal. The gateway attaches verified identity and checks the employee quota.
stages.why: Applications must authorise the employee, rather than trust the model.
stages.next: Next: Plan the two application decisions.

input.request: Schedule a meeting with John and send him the latest proposal.

checks.text: Identity comes from enterprise authentication, never model-generated arguments.

stages.title: Plan the two application decisions
stages.what: The planner separates booking the calendar slot from finding and sharing a proposal. It tracks both results.
stages.why: One function cannot coordinate these two domains.
stages.next: Next: Return a job ID and queue the plan.

checks.text: A multi-step plan is bounded; no unlimited tool loop.

stages.title: Discover only the relevant capabilities
stages.what: The registry selects the calendar and document MCP servers. Their tool descriptions enter this request context.
stages.why: Loading all 100+ applications would waste prompt space and weaken selection.
stages.next: Next: Select functions and validate their arguments.

checks.text: Only task-relevant tool schemas are loaded.

stages.title: Select functions and validate their arguments
stages.what: The model chooses the exposed booking and proposal tools. The application validates the typed arguments before dispatch.
stages.why: Function calling decides what to invoke; it does not grant authority or replace the transport.
stages.next: Next: Book through the calendar application.

checks.text: Schema validation is a design addition in this example; downstream permissions still decide access.

stages.title: Book through the calendar application
stages.what: The calendar connector uses the application transport to book a slot. The calendar checks the employee identity before writing.
stages.why: The backend remains the authority even when the model selected the call.
stages.next: Next: Stop sharing at the document permission check.

checks.text: The calendar grants the employee the required write permission.

stages.title: Share the permitted proposal
stages.what: The document application finds the latest proposal visible to the employee and permits sharing with John. It returns the application result.
stages.why: Discovery of a tool is different from permission to read or share its data.
stages.next: Next: Return both application outcomes.

checks.text: Both read access and permitted sharing are checked by the application.

stages.title: Return both application outcomes
stages.what: The trace records selected tools, application results, latency and errors. The response reports what each application actually did.
stages.why: A multi-step request may partly succeed; one blanket success would hide failures.
stages.next: The calendar booked the meeting and the document application shared the proposal.

checks.text: Trace metadata should support debugging without exposing unnecessary sensitive payloads.

scenarios.label: Document sharing is denied
scenarios.outcome: The meeting remains booked. The proposal was not shared; the employee sees the partial result.

stages.what: The document application denies sharing the proposal. The trace records a partial result and the response states that the meeting already exists.

input.request: Create a Jira ticket for the broken monitor.

checks.text: Identity comes from enterprise authentication, never model-generated arguments.

stages.title: Select the known ticket function
stages.what: For a single ticket the model selects the known create-ticket function. It does not build a multi-domain plan.
stages.why: Planning overhead buys nothing for one deterministic operation.
stages.next: Next: Execute against the ticket backend.

input.request: Create a Jira ticket for the broken monitor.

checks.text: The ticket schema is validated before the transport call.

stages.title: Execute against the ticket backend
stages.what: The connector calls the ticket application with the employee identity. The application checks create permission and returns its ticket ID.
stages.why: REST executes the choice the model made; the two are different layers.
stages.next: Next: Trace the single result.

checks.text: The backend validates employee permission.

stages.title: Trace the single result
stages.what: The trace records the tool result and the response gives the ticket ID. No planner or broad tool discovery was required.
stages.why: A short workflow should stay short.
stages.next: The application returns one created ticket; the planner is skipped.

checks.text: Record tool latency and errors.

stages.title: Return a job ID and queue the plan
stages.what: The gateway returns task accepted with a job ID. A worker will execute the plan asynchronously.
stages.why: Long workflows should not hold an interactive request open.
stages.next: Next: Record the pending execution.

checks.text: Acceptance is distinct from execution or completion.

stages.title: Record the pending execution
stages.what: The trace records the accepted job and its pending application steps. A later status update must use the actual application outcomes.
stages.why: Queueing work is not proof that a business action happened.
stages.next: The employee has job-42 and a running status. No meeting or document action is claimed complete.

checks.text: Observe worker backlog and per-application errors.

revision.pitch: I would put enterprise identity and a gateway in front of every request. The applications trust that identity, not the model. For a simple ticket, function calling chooses the tool and the backend transport executes it. For a request across calendar and documents, a planner coordinates the decisions. A tool registry loads only the relevant MCP servers, so we do not place thousands of tool schemas in every prompt. MCP makes those capabilities discoverable; it does not replace REST, SOAP or SQL underneath. Each backend checks the employee permissions before reading or writing. Long work returns a job ID and runs asynchronously. I would trace tool selection, application results, errors, latency and cost, and report partial success honestly. This case goes deep on integration. It leaves RAG, memory and approval to the support-assistant design.
revision.flow: Identity → gateway → optional planner → relevant tool discovery → function choice → application transport and authorisation → traced results
requirements: Natural-language conversation, reads and writes across 100+ applications, multi-step workflows, tool execution and enterprise authentication.
Availability, security, extensibility, maintainability and easy application onboarding at the scenario scale.
discovery: Does every employee see the same data?
revision.tradeoff: Dynamic tool discovery reduces prompt size but makes registry quality and permission-aware exposure important. A planner helps multi-domain work and is overhead for a single ticket.
revision.failure: The calendar may succeed while document sharing is denied. Report the partial outcome; the source does not define a cross-application transaction.
ops: Load relevant MCP servers rather than all applications. Keep stateless services and quotas; the source scale is an assumption.
Run long workflows asynchronously with job IDs. Trace application calls rather than promising one universal response time.
Bound model/tool loops and account for each application call. Reuse caches only within the correct identity scope.
Exercise simple and multi-domain requests, application denials, tool-selection quality and partial completion.
revision.remember: REST executes. Function calling decides. MCP discovers. The planner coordinates.
